passages.t: ‘Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man?’, and the olive tree
passages.happening:
The heading ties this psalm to a dark day in David's life. It is “A Maskil of David. After Doeg the Edomite went to Saul and told him, ‘David has gone to the house of Ahimelech’” (verse 1).

The psalm speaks straight to a powerful man. “Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? The loving devotion of God endures all day long” (verse 1). His weapon is his tongue. “Your tongue devises destruction like a sharpened razor, O worker of deceit” (verse 2). “You love every word that devours” (verse 4).

His end is sure. “Surely God will bring you down to everlasting ruin” (verse 5). Others will look and say, “Look at the man who did not make God his refuge, but trusted in the abundance of his wealth” (verse 7).

Then the psalmist sets himself beside him. “But I am like an olive tree flourishing in the house of God; I trust in the loving devotion of God forever and ever” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The story is in 1 Samuel 21 and 22. Running from Saul, David was given bread and Goliath's sword by the priest Ahimelech at the town of Nob. Doeg, Saul's chief shepherd, saw it and told Saul. When Saul's own guards refused to kill the priests, Doeg did it. “On that day he killed eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod” (1 Samuel 22:18). David later said, “I myself am responsible for the lives of everyone in your father’s house” (1 Samuel 22:22).

This is the first of several psalms in Book Two whose headings tie them to David's years on the run from Saul (52, 54, 56, 57, 59). The book page explains what the headings are and how readers weigh them.

An olive tree can live for centuries and grow back from its roots when cut down. It gave oil for food, light and anointing. The wicked man is torn ‘from your tent’ and uprooted (verse 5). The faithful man is rooted.
passages.later:
The Bible often warns about the tongue. James writes that the rich “will pass away like a flower of the field” (James 1:10), and spends a whole chapter on the harm words can do (James 3).

Israel itself was once called “a flourishing olive tree” (Jeremiah 11:16). Paul uses the olive tree to picture God's people, with new branches grafted in (Romans 11:17).
passages.hard: Is it right for the righteous to mock the fallen man (verse 6)? They first “see and fear” (verse 6), which suggests awe at God's justice, not spite. Their words read more like a lesson than a jeer: look where trusting wealth leads. Still, Proverbs says, “Do not gloat when your enemy falls” (Proverbs 24:17), and Jesus told his followers to love their enemies. The book page's part on the cursing psalms sets out how Christians read lines like this.
passages.asks:
Doeg's evil started with words. He told the truth, in a way, but he told it to destroy. Ask yourself what your words are for. Do they build up, or do they devour?

And notice the two trees in this psalm. One man trusts his wealth and is uprooted. The other trusts God's loving devotion and grows. Where are your roots?
